papers.abstract: Latent world models enable goal-directed planning from offline visual data, but prediction alone does not specify which action-related distinctions their representations should preserve. Inverse dynamics provides auxiliary supervision, yet squared-error action regression rewards additional information only through changes in the conditional action mean. We propose Contrastive Identification of Actions (CIA), which identifies the executed action among alternatives sampled from a history-conditioned behavior proposal. Comparing actions plausible in the same context targets information supplied by the next latent beyond history. Under exact behavior matching, we show that CIA can reward action information that leaves optimal inverse-regression error unchanged, and verify this distinction through a controlled learning example. CIA achieves higher planner-averaged mean success than the base world model and a regression inverse-dynamics baseline across five visual control benchmarks, without modifying the planner.
authors: Hayeong Lee, Youngjun Suh. Byung-Jun Lee
bullets: Problem: Prediction alone does not ensure representations retain the action distinctions needed for planning.
Method: Identify the executed action against alternatives sampled from a history-conditioned behavior proposal.
Key insight: CIA captures action information beyond the conditional action mean, including information invisible to squared-error regression.
Evidence: A controlled example verifies this distinction, and CIA improves planner-averaged mean success over both a base world model and a regression inverse-dynamics baseline.
Scope: Results are evaluated on five visual control benchmarks without changing the planner.

papers.abstract: Learning latent actions from unlabeled video sequences offers a promising way to acquire reusable action representations without relying on embodiment-specific control annotations. However, existing latent-action pretraining approaches commonly couple the modeling of visual transitions with action inference, directly mapping paired observations or derived transition cues into latent action codes. This formulation leaves two distinct tasks entangled: characterizing the relational structure of an observed transition and abstracting it into a compact action representation. We propose RELACT, a relation-first framework that explicitly separates transition relation modeling from predictive action abstraction. RELACT first constructs a structured relation representation $R$ that captures how visual elements and their interactions evolve across observations. It then infers a compact, state-conditioned stochastic latent action $U$, whose predictive effects are learned through action-conditioned latent dynamics. The resulting action representation can be grounded in native control spaces for model-based planning or used to supervise downstream embodied policies. Extensive experiments across in-domain and out-of-domain image-goal navigation, goal-conditioned manipulation, and downstream policy adaptation demonstrate improved predictive action representations and consistent gains in planning and control, supporting the effectiveness and generality of relation-first latent action pretraining.
authors: Boning Zhang, Junyu Gao, Changsheng Xu
bullets: Addresses the entanglement of transition understanding and action inference in existing methods.
Builds a structured relation representation capturing evolving visual elements and interactions.
Infers compact, state-conditioned stochastic latent actions with action-conditioned latent dynamics.
Supports grounding actions in control spaces for planning and supervising embodied policies.
Experiments across navigation, manipulation, and policy adaptation show improved action representations and consistent planning/control gains.

(b) Predictive action abstraction: A state-conditioned posterior infers a compact latent action U from the current visual state Zt and the relation R. papers.abstract: Latent action models (LAMs) learn action-like latents from unlabeled video by coupling frame-pair inference with latent-conditioned prediction, enabling policy and world-model pretraining. However, what the latent must explain depends on the representation space used for action inference and transition prediction. When this space entangles the agent's evolving physical state with visual context, such as background and persistent agent appearance, inferred latents can encode information unrelated to the agent's actions. To address this challenge, we propose Agent-State LAM, which jointly learns a compact agent-state representation and latent actions modeling its transitions. The compact state aggregates dense visual features into a shared space for both action inference and forward prediction. To guide what this state retains, we introduce spatially matched temporal discrimination (SMTD), which trains the state to distinguish its source frame from nearby frames through spatially flexible matching with frozen local visual features. Rather than comparing global frame representations, SMTD scores each frame by emphasizing its strongest local feature matches across spatial locations. This scoring allows background and persistent agent appearance to remain matched across frames despite displacement, making these shared cues less informative for identifying the source frame and encouraging the representation to capture the agent's evolving physical state. Extensive experiments on distracting control tasks and six real robot video datasets demonstrate improved action recovery, downstream control, and world-model prediction. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Mid-Push/Agent-State-LAM.
authors: Shaoan Xie, Fan Feng, Peiyuan Zhu, Peter Spirtes, Kun Zhang
bullets: LAMs can encode background and persistent appearance when action inference and prediction use entangled visual representations.
The method jointly learns a compact agent-state representation and latent actions that model state transitions.
Spatially matched temporal discrimination (SMTD) uses flexible local feature matching to deemphasize shared background and appearance cues.
Experiments on distracting control tasks and six real-robot video datasets show improved action recovery, downstream control, and world-model prediction.
The approach targets settings where visual context distracts from the agent’s physical state.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) typically adapt large pretrained video generators to jointly predict future observations and robot actions, incurring substantial training and deployment costs. However, it remains unclear which future representations a policy actually needs and how compactly they can be represented. Our probing study shows that complementary future representations can be compressed into a few tokens while retaining most of their action-decoding performance. Motivated by this finding, we introduce LeanWAM, a latent WAM that transfers video priors from a frozen video generator to a lightweight policy via two-stage training. In the first stage, a Future Extractor compresses observed transitions into 32 predictive tokens. These tokens condition the frozen generator and are jointly shaped by action, RGB, semantic, and geometric supervision, while a compact readout of the generator's hidden states supplies complementary world tokens. The second stage distills both representations into the policy, which learns to predict them from current observations while generating actions. With 1.4B parameters and no large-scale embodied pretraining, LeanWAM outperforms strong vision-language-action (VLA) and WAM baselines on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin~2.0. It predicts an action chunk in 25.1\,ms on an A100 GPU, 12.3--41.5$\times$ faster than representative WAMs. These results demonstrate that compact predictive supervision can transfer video priors to robust and efficient control.
authors: Shaolong Li, Hongze Fu, Joyce Chai, Yinpei Dai
bullets: WAMs can retain most action-decoding ability using only a few compressed future-representation tokens.
A two-stage pipeline transfers priors from a frozen video generator to a lightweight policy.
The method uses 32 predictive tokens plus complementary hidden-state world tokens, shaped by action, RGB, semantic, and geometric supervision.
LeanWAM outperforms strong VLA and WAM baselines on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0.
It predicts action chunks in 25.1 ms on an A100, reported as 12.3–41.5× faster than representative WAMs.

papers.abstract: World action model (WAM) is a promising paradigm for visuomotor control by jointly modeling world dynamics and actions. Notably, existing WAMs often rely on large generative models and iterative sampling which incur substantial latency for action generation, limiting real-time deployment. In particular, there are two root causes of inefficiency in conventional flow matching or diffusion based action models in WAMs: 1) transporting uninformative Gaussian noise into precise actions necessitating multiple ODE steps, and 2) repeatedly injecting task context through expensive cross-attention modules. Our key insight is that jointly learning and aligning the source and action manifolds streamlines the transport between them, substantially accelerating action generation. Building on this insight, we introduce VITA-WAM, a WAM architecture with manifold-aligned flow-matching (VITA flow matching) that directly transports latent observation representations containing visual, language, and proprioceptive information into latent actions. More specifically, a flow latent alignment (FLA) mechanism is employed to facilitate manifold alignment between latent observation and action representations, enabling accurate generation with few ODE steps. The resulting architecture also eliminates costly attention for observation conditioning during repeated denoising steps. Notably, with a single ODE step, VITA-WAM outperforms 10-step FastWAM by 21.47 pp on LIBERO-Plus and by 1.65 pp on LIBERO, achieving these gains through the FLA objective without distillation, while inferring at 55.67~ms latency, a $2.10\times$ speedup compared to FastWAM.
authors: Boqi Zhao, Dechen Gao, Hanchu Zhou, Hang Wang, Junshan Zhang
bullets: Addresses the latency of conventional diffusion- or flow-matching-based world-action models caused by noise-to-action transport and repeated cross-attention.
Directly transports latent visual, language, and proprioceptive observation representations into latent actions.
Uses flow latent alignment (FLA) to align observation and action manifolds and support accurate generation with few ODE steps.
With one ODE step, it outperforms 10-step FastWAM by 21.47 percentage points on LIBERO-Plus and 1.65 points on LIBERO.
Achieves 55.67 ms inference latency, a 2.10× speedup over FastWAM, without distillation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Illustration of VITA-WAM architecture. 1) During training (top), a Q-Former fuses visual, language and proprioception into a latent source z0, where the visual signal is the output of the video DiT supervised by video flow matching. The action encoder maps the action chunk into a target latent z1. The source and target representations are jointly learned with VITA flow matching through FM, AE and FLA objectives, with FLA supervising the action chunk decoded from the ODE-generated latent. 2) During inference (bottom), a single video DiT forward pass extracts current-observation features, which are fused with language and proprioception by the Q-Former to construct the source latent z0. The action DiT then performs conditioningfree ODE integration starting from z0 to generate the action latent ẑ1, which is decoded into an action chunk.

Figure 6: Training and inference architecture of VITA-WAM (visual conditioning). The Q-Former constructs the source latent from visual observations, language, and proprioception. During ODE integration, the action DiT additionally uses mixed video–action attention with cached video K/V. The action decoder converts the generated latent into an action chunk.

Figure 1: Comparing conventional flow matching (left) vs. VITA flow matching (right). Conventional flow matching learns to transport Gaussian noise to the target manifold, necessitating multiple ODE steps. VITA flow matching (right) jointly learns and aligns the source and target representation manifolds with the Flow Latent Alignment (FLA) mechanism, thus enabling generation with simplified transport paths and fewer ODE steps. VITA-WAM employs VITA flow matching, significantly improving the efficiency of WAM action generation.

papers.abstract: World models facilitate planning and control in robotic manipulation by enabling agents to anticipate the consequences of their actions. However, they typically rely on action-labelled interaction data that is costly to acquire and difficult to scale. These models are also often tied to the specific embodiment they were trained on, limiting transferability to previously unseen robot morphologies. We introduce a 3D latent-action world model that learns continuous action representations directly from point-cloud observations of retargeted human manipulation demonstrations. A contrastive objective is used to encourage consistent representations of motion across embodiments. The resulting unified latent action space serves directly as the search space for model-predictive control, where sampled latent actions condition particle-based future predictions. Executable robot commands are then recovered from the predicted geometric motion without requiring an embodiment-specific action decoder. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that the learned latent actions exhibit controllable and compositional motion, transfer to unseen robot embodiments, and support zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries. Following task-agnostic adaptation, our model achieves 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, compared with DexWM's reported 72%, 58%, and 28%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot real-world manipulation with an unseen dexterous hand, achieving an 86% success rate across 50 trials on five diverse tasks involving pushing, grasping, and lifting everyday objects. These results highlight the potential of geometry-grounded latent actions as a unified, transferable interface for world-model-based robotic manipulation. Project materials, including demonstration videos and source code, are available at https://vinaymohan0409.github.io/DexLatentWorld/.
authors: Vinay Udit Mohan, Xuchuan Huang, Rolandos Alexandros Potamias
bullets: Addresses the high cost of action-labelled data and poor transferability of embodiment-specific world models.
Learns continuous latent actions from point-cloud observations using retargeted human demonstrations and a contrastive cross-embodiment objective.
Uses latent actions directly for model-predictive control with particle-based future prediction; executable commands are recovered from predicted geometric motion.
Reports 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, and 86% success across 50 real-world trials on five tasks with an unseen dexterous hand.
Demonstrates controllable, compositional, and transferable motion, including zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries.

papers.title: DexLatentWorld: 3D Cross-Embodiment Latent Action World Models for Zero-Shot Robotic Manipulation

papers.abstract: Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot recordings, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without a shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverse- and forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate high-fidelity dynamics, yet represent them densely, entangled across all layers. Viewing the world model as a LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. We further propose a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it never generates video. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With a 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it is competitive on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading leaderboard entries. On real robots, it improves over the pi_0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages use only public data and a publicly released world model.
authors: Qinyue Li, Weijie Qiao, Qingyi Tao, Zerui Gong, Zhe Yang, Quanzhou Li, Taolin Zhang, Jinglin He, Zhonghua Wu, Chen Change Loy
bullets: Addresses learning actions from diverse videos that lack actions or share no common action space.
Uses one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both inverse- and forward-dynamics models, connected by learnable dynamics registers.
Trains on counterfactual video pairs differing only in motion to distill compact latent actions without video generation.
Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on LARY for action classification and control, and transfer motion across robots, scenes, and human-to-robot settings.
The PAWlicy pretraining paradigm achieves a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and improves over pi_0.5 on both evaluated real-robot tasks.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human manipulation data offer a scalable resource for training dexterous robot policies. However, how effectively robots can learn and benefit from these data remains unclear due to the embodiment gap between humans and robots. We present EgoStudy, a systematic, controlled study of egocentric data for robot learning. Holding the robot dataset fixed, we vary the scale and diversity of egocentric data, data processing strategies, and co-training configurations. We investigate three questions: (1) Which data processing and pretraining choices most effectively exploit egocentric data? (2) Which components of robot action prediction benefit most from scaling these data? (3) How do scaling effects differ between vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs)? Our experiments yield three main findings. First, data diversity, alignment between trajectories, and detailed language annotations are key factors in effective transfer. Second, scaling egocentric data yields larger gains in predicting end-effector translation than in predicting fine-grained finger movements. Third, WAMs perform better when egocentric data are limited, whereas VLAs exhibit greater gains as the amount of egocentric data increases. Together, these findings provide practical guidance on processing and using egocentric data to train VLAs and WAMs, while clarifying the benefits and limitations of scaling these data.
authors: Puzhen Yuan, Yanjiang Guo, Yichen Liu, Xiang Zhu, Qingzhou Lu, Chenxin Liu, Tun Ban, Haodong Yan, Zhide Zhong, Jianyu Chen
bullets: Egocentric data transfer improves with greater diversity, trajectory alignment, and detailed language annotations.
Scaling primarily benefits end-effector translation prediction rather than fine-grained finger movement.
WAMs perform better with limited egocentric data, while VLAs gain more as egocentric data scale increases.
The study offers practical guidance for processing and co-training egocentric and robot data.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Which data processing and co-training designs improve transfer? Complete episodes, detailed captions, and the dataset diversity yield lower wrist translation error on both robot holdouts for both model families. This indicates that data diversity and alignment between trajectories and detailed language annotations are key factors in effective transfer. Moreover, fixed-step sampling yields lower error for the VLA, and event-level sampling yields lower error for the WAM.

Figure 7. Which action components benefit most from scaling egocentric data? We measure mean squared error (MSE) separately for wrist translation, wrist rotation, and fingertip pose on high-quality, held-out robot trajectories. Across both robot domains and model families, wrist translation MSE generally decreases as egocentric data scale, while wrist rotation and fingertip pose errors show no consistent decline. We hypothesize that due to human–robot embodiment gap and errors in estimating actions limit transfer primarily to large-scale motions such as wrist translation, with less benefit for the finger movements and wrist rotations.

Figure 4. Does scaling egocentric data improve robot learning? We pretrain the VLA (left) and WAM (right) with 1%, 3%, 10%, 30%, and 100% of the egocentric human data while keeping robot training exposure and the optimization budget fixed. We evaluate wrist translation MSE on held-out trajectories from Bimanual XHand and RoboCasa-GR1. All four model–domain pairs show a consistent downward trend, indicating effective human-to-robot transfer in EgoStudy.

Figure 6. Do pretraining gains carry over to robot control? RoboCasa-GR1 task success increases after posttraining for both model families, consistent with the decrease in pretraining validation loss. Gray dashed lines mark the corresponding baselines without pretraining.

Figure 9. How does backbone choice affect scaling gains between VLA and WAM? The wrist translation error decreases to the same extent across different VLAs, indicating that the 4B backbone is already capable of effectively extracting features shared between the egocentric and robot data. When the backbone of WAM is changed to 5B, its human-to-robot capability declines indicating that WAM relies more heavily on a powerful video backbone to assimilate egocentric data.

Figure 8. How do VLA and WAM visual features change with scale? As egocentric data scale, relative separation R between human and robot features decreases in both robot domains for the VLA but shows no consistent decrease across the WAM layers examined. We hypothesize that human and robot features align more closely in our VLA because it only needs to output actions in a shared action space. Our WAM must also predict future video, which may encourage it to retain visual differences between human and robot hands.

Figure 3. Pretraining samples allocation. Egocentric datasets receive 75% of samples, with probabilities proportional to the square root of their filtered durations; VITRA aggregates three subsets. The sampling probabilities of Bimanual XHand (20%) and RoboCasa-GR1 (5%) are fixed across experiments.
Figure 2. Red points and arrows indicate positions and orientations (omitting 2 axes for clarity), respectively, in shared dexterous action space and different embodiments.

papers.abstract: Distilling localization knowledge into compact detection transformers (DETRs) requires consistent teacher-student query correspondence across decoder layers. However, in DETRs with encoder-based query selection, the teacher and student select top-K proposals independently. Same-rank queries can originate from different spatial locations and correspond to different objects, making rank-based layer-wise supervision unreliable. To address this problem, we propose Trajectory-Aligned Encoder-Decoder Distillation (TAED), a framework for knowledge transfer between DETRs of different capacities. Encoder feature distillation matches normalized multi-scale features to strengthen student representations and increase the number of teacher-student query pairs from the same encoder locations. Source-indexed query alignment pairs native queries from the same encoder locations and retains pairs associated with the same object for which the teacher provides reliable and more accurate final localization than the student. Trajectory-aligned localization distillation maintains these correspondences and uses teacher proposals and corresponding decoder-layer box predictions to guide student refinement, without introducing additional queries. On COCO, TAED improves DINO-R18 and two-stage Deformable DETR-R18 by 2.5 and 1.7 AP, respectively. Further gains on D-FINE and ECDet demonstrate applicability to recent real-time DETRs at no additional inference cost.
authors: Zilong He, Zhangchi Hu, Hebei Li, Yijun Pan, Yifan Zhao, Xiangyu Yu, Yansong Peng, Xinghao Wang, Dongsheng Jiang, Xiaoyan Sun
bullets: Addresses unreliable rank-based supervision caused by independently selected top-K proposals in teacher and student DETRs.
Distills normalized multi-scale encoder features to improve student representations and increase shared-location query matches.
Aligns native queries by source encoder index and keeps pairs where the teacher offers more accurate localization for the same object.
Transfers teacher proposal and decoder-layer box trajectories to guide student refinement without adding queries.
Improves DINO-R18 by 2.5 AP and two-stage Deformable DETR-R18 by 1.7 AP on COCO; also applies to D-FINE and ECDet without extra inference cost.

papers.abstract: World models support planning by predicting how the environment evolves under candidate actions. However, one-step predictive accuracy alone does not characterize multi-step planning utility, which depends on distinguishing candidate futures. This raises a natural question: How does latent transition geometry shape planning? We investigate this through an action-conditioned transition-field view, using curvature regularization as a controlled intervention. Across four continuous-control tasks, appropriately tuned regularization improves planning, while excessive regularization can be detrimental. By decomposing the transition field into affine and non-affine components, we find that regularization reduces action sensitivity mainly through the non-affine component. To assess its role in planning, we directly manipulate the non-affine action response in frozen models and show that it affects candidate selection and closed-loop success. Further analysis shows that curvature generally brings predicted futures closer together, while preserving more of the differences along the goal direction. This helps explain why the planning effects vary across tasks. We observe broadly consistent planning trends across five sampling- and gradient-based solvers on LeWM and similar rollout-geometry trends on DINO-WM. Qualitative attention visualizations reveal accompanying shifts toward task-relevant visual structure. Together, these findings clarify how latent transition geometry influences multi-step planning.
authors: Xuanya Zhu, Da Li, Xiatian Zhu
bullets: The study examines how curvature in action-conditioned latent transition fields affects multi-step planning.
Moderate curvature regularization improves planning across four continuous-control tasks, whereas excessive regularization can hurt.
Regularization mainly reduces action sensitivity in the non-affine transition component.
Directly manipulating non-affine action responses changes candidate selection and closed-loop success in frozen models.
Curvature brings predicted futures closer together while preserving more goal-relevant differences, helping explain task-dependent effects across multiple planning solvers and world models.

papers.selection_reason: Studies how latent transition geometry affects action-conditioned planning in world models, directly fitting latent-action and interactive world-model interests.
papers.title: How Latent Transition Geometry Matters for Planning in World Models
papers.tldr: Latent transition geometry—not just one-step prediction accuracy—shapes how effectively world models distinguish and plan among candidate futures.

papers.abstract: Terraforming Mars is a long-horizon, action-conditioned control problem that requires predicting atmospheric responses to interventions over centuries to identify effective policies. This position paper argues that physics-regularized recurrent state-space world models are the most promising foundation for this setting. Data-driven climate emulators lack action-conditioning, and physics-based general circulation models (GCMs) are too expensive for policy search. Among learned world models, recurrent state-space architectures with physics constraints are better suited than transformer-based alternatives: they provide native uncertainty quantification through their stochastic-deterministic decomposition, remain stable under sparse non-terrestrial training data, and enforce physical consistency at each rollout step. To make this position concrete, we describe a potential architecture combining JEPA-inspired latent encoding, universal differential equation constraints, and a Dreamer-lineage planning head. We also introduce MarsWorld, an open benchmark proposal for intervention-conditioned planetary world models, and discuss broader implications and objections.
authors: Sameera S Kashyap, Akshitha Nagaraj, Razvan Marinescu
bullets: Terraforming requires long-horizon, action-conditioned predictions of atmospheric responses.
Climate emulators often lack intervention conditioning, while physics-based GCMs are too costly for policy search.
The paper favors recurrent state-space models over transformers for uncertainty estimation, sparse-data stability, and stepwise physical consistency.
A proposed design combines JEPA-inspired latent representations, universal differential equation constraints, and a Dreamer-style planning head.
The paper proposes MarsWorld, an open benchmark for intervention-conditioned planetary world models, but presents a position and architecture proposal rather than experimental validation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Proposed Mars atmospheric world model architecture. S1: A two-stage training strategy separates synthetic pre-training data (MCD v6.1) from observational fine-tuning sources (EMARS, OpenMARS; with TES/MCS as the underlying retrievals); intervention actions at enter the transition model as continuous vectors. S2: A state encoder maps atmospheric fields to a latent z; PINN constraints and UDE residuals regularize the latent and downstream dynamics, merged at the concatenation node. S3: An RSSM propagates stochastic latent zt and recurrent memory ht under action-conditioned transitions ρ(z | h, a) with physics enforced at every step; ht is updated from (ht−1, zt−1, at−1) via the recurrent backbone. S4: An actor-critic head trains within imagined latent rollouts; the actor π(a | z, h) outputs intervention policies, the critic V (z, h) estimates returns from (∆P,∆T,∆O2), and a decoder reconstructs gridded fields against EMARS as an auxiliary signal. S5: Outputs are a learned policy trajectory, a long-horizon atmospheric forecast, and a rollout uncertainty map from stochastic latent samples.

Table 1: Requirements for Mars terraforming simulation vs. existing systems. (i) Mars physical accuracy; (ii) tractable for policy search; (iii) action-conditioned rollouts; (iv) century-scale stability; (v) trainable on sparse non-terrestrial data.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes action-conditioned recurrent state-space world models for long-horizon planetary control, directly fitting interactive and latent-action world-model interests.
papers.title: World Models Are the Right Foundation for Simulating Mars Terraforming
papers.tldr: Physics-regularized recurrent world models are proposed as a practical foundation for learning and planning Mars-terraforming interventions over centuries.

papers.abstract: We introduce MotionPort, which learns low-dimensional latent representations of body motion for accurate dynamics prediction and effective long-horizon planning. Existing world-model planners often search over action representations learned for prediction, yet we show that predictive accuracy alone does not ensure that optimization can discover successful trajectories. MotionPort addresses this mismatch by representing body trajectories rather than action chunks and organizing the search space by motion similarity, helping predicted improvements translate into successful execution. Without fine-tuning state encoders, MotionPort raises average goal-reaching success from 37.9% to 87.8% across three backbones and seven settings in four domains. On the evaluated AntMaze-OGBench tasks, it achieves 72% success, compared with 4% for the strongest baseline.
authors: Renhao Zhang, Abhranil Chandra, Bruno Castro da Silva
bullets: Predictive accuracy alone may not yield an action-search space that supports successful trajectory optimization.
MotionPort represents body trajectories and aligns the latent search space with motion similarity.
It requires no fine-tuning of state encoders.
Across three backbones and seven settings in four domains, average goal-reaching success increases from 37.9% to 87.8%.
On evaluated AntMaze-OGBench tasks, MotionPort achieves 72% success versus 4% for the strongest baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Learning and planning with MotionPort. papers.tldr: MotionPort improves long-horizon world-model planning by organizing low-dimensional body-motion trajectories around geometric similarity rather than relying solely on predictive action representations.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in physics-based humanoid control enable teams of varying sizes to coordinate their movements and cooperatively transport shared objects. However, adapting learned cooperative behaviors to unseen environmental constraints remains challenging, particularly when obstacles require coordinated detours and changes in team configuration. We propose CarlHOI, a counterfactual predictive imagination framework built upon a counterfactual-anchored relational latent world model (CarlWM) for human-object interaction (HOI), enabling multi-humanoid teams to adapt to unseen environmental constraints without retraining their underlying cooperative control policies. CarlHOI explicitly represents the shared object, individual humanoids, and environmental obstacles as interacting entities. Trained offline using counterfactual simulator rollouts, the model imagines alternative collective futures under different shared waypoint commands, predicting how the coupled humanoid team and object would respond. By evaluating these imagined outcomes through predicted progress, failure, and contact risks, and long-horizon value estimates, CarlHOI selects adaptive guidance commands while preserving the pretrained cooperative controller. We introduce a benchmark comprising three challenging obstacle-constrained transport tasks to evaluate adaptation and generalization. Despite being trained exclusively with four humanoids, our model generalizes without retraining to teams of two to ten humanoids, unseen obstacle geometries and placements, unseen objects, and novel combinations of environmental constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved cooperative transport success over evaluated baselines across diverse configurations. Results highlight the potential of counterfactual predictive imagination to extend pretrained multi-humanoid cooperative skills beyond their original training conditions.
bullets: Targets cooperative transport in environments requiring obstacle detours and changing team configurations.
Models humanoids, shared objects, and obstacles as interacting entities in a relational latent world model.
Imagines outcomes of alternative waypoint commands using offline counterfactual simulator rollouts.
Selects guidance commands using predicted progress, failure, contact risk, and long-horizon value.

Evaluated on three obstacle-constrained transport tasks, with generalization from four-humanoid training to teams of two to ten and unseen configurations; experiments report improved success over evaluated baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Uses a counterfactual latent world model for multi-humanoid cooperative manipulation, fitting robot learning and interactive/latent action world models.
papers.title: CarlHOI: Counterfactual Predictive Imagination for Generalizable Multi-Humanoid Object Interaction under Constrained Environments
papers.tldr: CarlHOI uses counterfactual world-model predictions to adapt pretrained multi-humanoid object-transport skills to unseen obstacles, team sizes, objects, and constraints without retraining.

papers.abstract: Sequence models trained on game moves have been shown to encode world models, with structured linear probes revealing the underlying game states. World models, however, are inherently dynamic: in deterministic board games, a set of rules constrain how states evolve over time. We therefore ask if and how OthelloGPT, a transformer trained only on Othello move sequences, manifests the rules of the game in its activation space. We divide the rules of Othello, and symmetrically their violations, into three classes: placing a disc on an empty square (R1), flanking an opponent's disc (R2), and moving in turn (R3). We find that linear probes accurately separate legal from illegal moves, and also distinguish between the three kinds of rule violations. We introduce an unsupervised rule-violation detector based on the step length of activations between consecutive moves, which identifies illegal moves above chance. We further improve our detection metric by computing step length in the latent space of select sparse autoencoders. Together, we find that OthelloGPT follows game rules of Othello to a large extent, and that we can detect rule violations using structured detectors on model activations.
authors: David L. Cao, Sai Sumedh R. Hindupur, Demba Ba
bullets: Linear probes separate legal from illegal moves in activation space.
Probes distinguish violations involving placement, flanking, and turn order.
An unsupervised detector uses activation step lengths between consecutive moves to identify illegal moves above chance.
Measuring step length in selected sparse-autoencoder latent spaces improves detection.
The study finds that OthelloGPT follows Othello’s rules to a large extent.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates how a game-playing transformer (OthelloGPT) encodes game rules and dynamics in its latent space, introducing unsupervised detectors for rule violations.
papers.title: From States to Dynamics: Detecting Rule Violations in OthelloGPT

papers.abstract: World-action models learn from future prediction, but accessing their future representations directly at test time can require costly frame generation. Methods that generate future frames before planning incur additional forward passes, while future co-training methods omit explicit future predictions at inference. We introduce \method, a planner that reads the hidden states of masked future tokens without decoding future frames. We pretrain MMaDA-Parallel-M on driving video using frame-level masked world modeling, which predicts a masked suffix of future frames and explicitly includes inputs with all future frames masked. Learned planning queries attend to these masked positions and the observed context, and a continuous head predicts the trajectory in the same forward pass. With a single front camera, \method reaches 92.0 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 89.3 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, with an end-to-end latency of 60.3\,ms.
authors: Ziyu Zhao, Casey Sun, Zeyu Wang, Shicong Ma, Emily T Zhang, Cheng Lu
bullets: Addresses the inference cost of generating future frames before planning.
Pretrains a masked world model on driving video, including inputs where all future frames are masked.
Uses planning queries over masked future states and observed context, with a continuous trajectory head in one forward pass.
Achieves 92.0 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 89.3 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 using a single front camera.
Runs with 60.3 ms end-to-end latency.

papers.abstract: Marine robots face partial observability, non-stationary dynamics, and sparse communication, motivating WMs that learn compact predictive states for planning. This review develops a functional taxonomy of WMs for ocean engineering, focusing on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) and AdaJEPA's test-time adaptation within model predictive control, mapping them to navigation, adaptive sampling, digital twins, and biodiversity monitoring, and separating demonstrated evidence from prospective applications. The synthesis identifies key Gaps: benchmarks, uncertainty calibration, safe adaptation and proposes a research agenda for physics-informed, deployment-adaptive marine WMs validated through simulation and field missions.
authors: Basma Dokkara, Esteban W. G. Cluab, Luiz M. G. Goncalves, Paolo Spagnolo, Cosimo Distante
bullets: Marine robots must operate under partial observability, changing dynamics, and limited communication.
It provides a functional taxonomy spanning navigation, adaptive sampling, digital twins, and biodiversity monitoring.

It distinguishes demonstrated evidence from prospective applications.
Key gaps include benchmarks, uncertainty calibration, and safe adaptation; it proposes physics-informed, deployment-adaptive validation in simulation and field missions.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) leverage the world knowledge of video generation models to improve action generation by aligning visual prediction with action prediction. However, their prediction overhead prevents real-time deployment on edge devices, and they usually lack an effective long-term memory. We introduce SANA-Robot, a 4.5B WAM with minute-level memory that runs in real time on edge devices, built on the following core designs: (1) hybrid memory at constant cost: our WAM relies on linear attention to maintain a global memory with a fixed-size state, and on sliding window softmax attention layers that propagate previous information, enabling high success rates on tasks requiring whole-episode memory while keeping an efficient and constant inference speed; (2) a unified model: by dynamically applying different noise levels to action and video tokens, SANA-Robot can serve not only as a policy but also as a world simulator; (3) a full-stack infrastructure for both memory training and inference, including efficient data packing and shuffling as well as memory-phase-based asynchronous execution. SANA-Robot achieves the best performance on the memory dimension of RoboDojo among models of medium size (about 5B) and the highest success rates on LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro and LIBERO-Max. In real-world deployment, SANA-Robot takes 135 ms per action chunk on an RTX 5090 with FP8 GEMMs and 115 ms with NVFP4 GEMMs, and achieves closed-loop, real-time asynchronous robot control at 30 Hz on edge devices, demonstrating both the efficiency and the effectiveness of SANA-Robot. Project page: https://nvlabs.github.io/Sana/Robot/
authors: Yuyang Zhao, Zekai Li, Yicheng Pan, Jiaming Tang, Zhuoyang Zhang, Jiaxu Xing, Moritz Reuss, Quanquan Peng, Junsong Chen, Enze Xie, Zhijian Liu, Song Han
bullets: Addresses WAM inference overhead and weak long-term memory for real-time, whole-episode robot tasks.
Uses linear attention for fixed-size global memory plus sliding-window softmax attention to propagate recent information at constant inference cost.
Dynamically assigns noise levels to action and video tokens, allowing one model to function as both a policy and a world simulator.
Includes infrastructure for memory training and inference, including efficient data handling and asynchronous memory-phase execution.
Reports strong memory-task performance and real-time deployment: 135 ms per action chunk on an RTX 5090 and 30 Hz control on edge devices.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | Overview of SANA-Robot, a unified world action model for FDM, IDM and policy. The video VAE encodes each camera view separately into the observation latent 𝑜 and the future video latent 𝑧, which enter the DiT together with the proprioception 𝑠 and the actions 𝑎; mRoPE places the views on a 2 × 2 grid of positions. The hybrid DiT stacks 8 blocks, each with three GDN layers and one softmax layer.

Figure 6 | Asynchronous execution of SANA-Robot-AR with 𝐶 = 32 and 𝑑 = 16. Request 𝑘 starts at step 𝑡𝑘, drops the first 𝑑 actions of its chunk and executes the next 𝐶 − 𝑑. (a) Direct RTC keeps a single memory and writes the 𝐶 − 𝑑 executed steps as one memory chunk, so its memory chunks are shorter than in training. (b) Memory RTC keeps one memory per phase 𝜙, whose chunks span 𝐶 steps as in training; at each 𝑡𝑘 (triangles), the window that has just ended is written into the memory of phase 𝜙𝑘, here every 16 steps, alternating between the two memories.

Figure 4 | Training SANA-Robot-AR on whole episodes. (a) Attention mask of chunk-causal teacher forcing for a window of four chunks: each row is a query and each column a key, and 𝑐𝑘, 𝑜𝑘 and 𝑛𝑘 denote the clean, observation (with proprioception) and noisy entries of chunk 𝑘. (b) Task-balanced ordering and one training step, schematic: the windows of each task are laid end to end on a line from 0 to 1 and sorted by their midpoints into one queue, which packing places on the GPUs without padding; length-bucketed padding wastes compute and skews the task mix of the step. (c) Per-step training loss when fine-tuning SANA-Robot-AR on RoboDojo: task-balanced ordering with packing halves the detrended loss fluctuation and shortens the median step time.

Figure 5 | Synchronous and asynchronous inference. (a) Synchronous execution: the robot idles for the latency 𝐿 of each request and then executes all 𝐶 actions of the new chunk. (b) Asynchronous execution: the request at 𝑡𝑘 is issued when 𝑑 actions of the current chunk remain and runs while the robot executes them; the first 𝑑 actions of chunk 𝑘 are dropped, and the robot executes the next 𝑃 = 𝐶 − 𝑑.

Figure 8 | Real-world capabilities. (a) SANA-Robot-base and SANA-Robot-AR; the dashed line marks random guessing. (b) Synchronous and asynchronous execution of SANA-Robot-AR with BF16 GEMMs: success rate, stall time per chunk and effective control frequency; the dashed line marks the 30 Hz cap of the controller. (c) Success on Tower of Hanoi and Air Hockey with BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 GEMMs.

Figure 9 | Memory designs on RoboDojo. The baseline memories are used to post-train SANA-Robot-base with the same data and initialization as SANA-Robot-AR; (b) reports the success rate on the memory tasks.

Figure 11 | Memory analysis of SANA-Robot-AR offline on RoboDojo. papers.abstract: Mobile embodied agents continuously alter their observations through their own motion, while external dynamics further shape future interactions. Different mobile embodied tasks therefore capture complementary patterns of state evolution, yet jointly learning world dynamics across such interactions remains less explored. We investigate this problem through Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) and Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT), which respectively involve navigation toward a stationary goal and interaction with a moving target. We propose WorldWeave, a cross-task world model that couples shared predictive dynamics with task-specific adaptation. Instead of conditioning state transitions on heterogeneous physical actions, WorldWeave learns latent actions from observed state changes via inverse-forward dynamics, establishing a shared transition representation across tasks. The resulting future-state predictions are adaptively integrated into task-specific representations for downstream decision making. Experiments across multiple VLN and EVT benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over specialized baselines.
authors: Xuan Yao, Jiahao Zhang, Rongjunchen Zhang, Kaixuan Huang, Junyu Gao, Changsheng Xu
bullets: Addresses underexplored cross-task world modeling for embodied agents whose actions and environments continually change future observations.
Uses inverse-forward dynamics to learn latent actions and a shared transition representation instead of relying on heterogeneous physical actions.
Combines shared predictive dynamics with task-specific adaptation for downstream navigation and tracking decisions.
Evaluations across multiple VLN and EVT benchmarks show consistent improvements over specialized baselines.

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) can improve pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies through imagined experiences. However, existing VLA-MBRL methods primarily rely on large-scale image or video generation world models, incurring large computational overhead. Latent world models offer a more efficient alternative but face two challenges: compounding errors during recursive prediction and incompatibility with VLAs' visual input interfaces. In this work, we propose LS-MBPO, a lightweight residual MBRL framework that leverages latent world models to improve upon pretrained VLAs. LS-MBPO introduces two key techniques: (1) Hierarchical Forcing, which combines dense causal supervision with autoregressive feedback to mitigate compounding prediction errors; and (2) Latent Subchunk Rollouts, which leverage action chunks from a frozen VLA policy and a latent residual policy for successive subchunk refinement, bridging the gap between latent imagination and VLA policy execution. We further introduce a Progress-Conditioned Branch-Start Curriculum that progressively shifts rollout starting points from later to earlier task stages, enabling effective policy learning from short imagined rollouts. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and a real-world ALOHA robot show that LS-MBPO achieves superior task performance and training efficiency compared to existing methods.
authors: Nan Tang, Han-Tao Zhang, Jing-Cheng Pang, Hao-Nan Wang, Hao-Xiang Ren, Yi-Fei Sheng, Jun-Yin Ye, Tian Xu, Fan-Ming Luo, Hao-Xin Lin, Yang Yu
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of image/video-based VLA model-based reinforcement learning.
Uses Hierarchical Forcing to mitigate compounding errors in recursive latent predictions.
Introduces Latent Subchunk Rollouts to connect latent imagination with frozen VLA action-chunk execution.
Applies a Progress-Conditioned Branch-Start Curriculum for learning from short imagined rollouts.
Reports strong task performance and training efficiency across LIBERO, RoboTwin, and a real-world ALOHA robot.

papers.abstract: Latent action models let a robot policy learn from video by turning the change between two frames into a training target. In egocentric video, a cup can move across the image because a hand pushes it or because the wearer turns. Both changes help predict the next frame, but only the first describes manipulation. During training, EgoLAM supervises the action code with measured wrist motion and supplies camera motion separately to the forward model. Even when the wearer turns while pushing a cup, the training target still describes how the hand pushed it. The action encoder pools object slots around each hand, and wrist translation and rotation can be decoded from the code in a common reference frame. Extracting a code then requires only two RGB frames. Alongside LARYBench classification and regression, we measure how much wrist motion a frozen code retains and how strongly it responds to a synthetic view or lighting change. EgoLAM has the highest hand-motion decoding score among eight evaluated models. Across three LIBERO suites, policies pretrained on its codes and fine-tuned on expert demonstrations achieve 79.38% mean success, 28.73 points above expert behavior cloning and 9.76 points above the strongest other latent action model in each suite on average.
authors: Ziyi Ding, Yiwei Wang, Zhongxing Wei, Xianxin Lai, Yechi Liu, Xiaodi Huang, Jinghua Hou, Xiaoquan Sun, Haijier Chen, Zhe Liu, Yinan Chen, Junqiao Zhao, Xiao-Ping Zhang, Jiayu Chen
bullets: Problem: Egocentric frame changes mix hand manipulation with camera motion, making action targets ambiguous.
Method: Supervises latent action codes with measured wrist translation and rotation while providing camera motion separately to the forward model.
Design: Pools object representations around each hand and decodes wrist motion in a shared reference frame; inference uses only two RGB frames.
Evaluation: Tests hand-motion retention and robustness to synthetic viewpoint and lighting changes, alongside LARYBench tasks.
Results: Achieves the highest hand-motion decoding score among eight models and 79.38% mean LIBERO success, outperforming behavior cloning and other latent-action models on average.

papers.abstract: If we optimize an image until a classifier is confident it shows a cat, we may get an adversarial example, not a cat. Planning with a latent world model is a similar search for actions whose predicted future is closest to the goal. Is the result a plan, or an adversarial example of the world model? We show that it can be either. On the released DINO-WM and LeWM, more iterations of the cross-entropy method (CEM) lower the predicted cost but lose up to half of the problems CEM had already solved. The model's own predictions do not reveal these failures. We propose a simple test that executes the plan after every iteration and counts the problems a planner solves and then loses. Unlike an image, a plan comes with its actions, which our round-trip check reads back from the predicted states with a small network, penalizing mismatches. The check reads back the sum of each block of five actions, the part that two consecutive predicted states determine. Without retraining the world model and at only 0.2% to 3.1% more planning time, it improves the widely used planners CEM and MPPI on three released world models, and gains more where planners lose more problems. Without replanning, success rises from 0.39 to 0.76 on Wall with DINO-WM and from 0.56 to 0.94 for MPPI on JEPA-WM. With replanning (MPC), it rises from 0.70 to 0.81 on Cube with LeWM.
authors: Huiyuan Tian, Chih-Yung Wen, Shijian Li
bullets: More CEM iterations can reduce predicted cost while causing planners to lose up to half of previously solved problems.
The world model’s predictions alone fail to reveal these planning failures.
The proposed check executes plans after each iteration and compares predicted actions with actions read back from predicted states.
It improves CEM and MPPI across three released world models with only 0.2%–3.1% additional planning time.
Reported success increases from 0.39 to 0.76 on Wall, 0.56 to 0.94 on JEPA-WM, and 0.70 to 0.81 with MPC on Cube.

figures.caption: Figure 1. A plan can be an adversarial example of the world model. The model cannot recognize it, and our round-trip check repairs the planner. (a) A mosaic of color blocks optimized against an ImageNet [13] classifier (ViT-B/16 [14]) is labeled a tabby cat with probability 0.99. (b) The standard CEM planner optimizes actions against DINO-WM [56]. Its plan reaches the goal after 10 iterations and becomes an adversarial example after 30. The model predicts that the final plan reaches the goal, but in the simulator it ends on the wrong side of the wall. (c) The same happens with LeWM [34], whose final plan drops the cube far from its target. With our round-trip check, the same planner’s final plans reach the goal, without retraining the world model and at only 0.2% and 3.1% more planning time.

Figure 3. The round-trip check. (a) The frozen predictor rolls out the candidate plans a of the planner, and the inverse-dynamics network gϕ reads the summed action of each block back from consecutive predicted states. Its residual r against the planned sums s(at) is added to the predicted cost ĉ with weight λ. (b) Decoded predicted states of the final plan of CEM and of the plan found with the check, with the residual r of each plan at the end of its row. Each circle compares the planned sum of a block with the sum that gϕ reads back, and its radius is the largest sum in the training data. The final plan of CEM asks for block sums that its own predicted states do not support, while the plan found with the check agrees with its prediction. (c) Many action sequences connect the same two predicted states, and only their sum is identifiable, so the check reads back this sum.

Figure 4. The same divergence for CEM with LeWM. We use 200 problems per task. (a, c) Success rate of the plan executed after each iteration. (b, d) Median cost of that plan, dashed as the model predicts it and solid as the simulator measures it. On both tasks the predicted cost of the plan of CEM keeps falling, while its true cost stops falling or rises, so the shaded gap between the two widens. With the round-trip check, the plan ends at a lower true cost and a higher success rate.

Figure 2. With the standard planner, planning longer makes the model more confident and the plan worse. The data are from DINO-WM on the Wall task with 148 problems. (a) With the standard CEM planner, the success rate peaks at 0.56 after 11 iterations and falls to 0.39 after 30, and with our round-trip check it rises to 0.76. (b) The median cost that the model predicts for the plan of CEM keeps falling, while the cost that the plan achieves in the simulator rises after iteration 11, and the shaded gap between the two widens. With the round-trip check, the true cost ends at less than a third of that of CEM. The dotted line marks iteration 11 in both panels.

Figure 5. The standard planners can end in adversarial plans, and the round-trip check finds plans that reach the goal. Each example shows the goal, the end of the final plan as the model predicts it and as it is executed, and the end of the plan found with the round-trip check. The predicted end is the nearest training frame, and a tick or a cross marks whether an end reaches the goal. In (a) the final plan of MPPI fails, and in (b) CEM solves the problem after 10 iterations and loses it after 30. The dotted circle marks the distance within which a problem counts as solved.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the reliability of latent world models by proposing a 'round-trip check' that validates plans against actual execution, improving planning robustness.
papers.title: A Plan or an Adversarial Example? A Round-Trip Check for Latent World Models
papers.tldr: A lightweight round-trip check detects adversarial plans in latent world models and substantially improves planning reliability with minimal extra cost.

papers.abstract: Motor decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) supports non-invasive brain-computer interfaces, yet existing methods either rely on costly cue-based trials and coarse categorical labels or use pretraining objectives that do not directly capture how movement unfolds, limiting their ability to learn transferable motor representations. To this end, we propose the Mind World Model (MWM), a framework that learns motor EEG representations from scalable naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations. MWM treats EEG observed up to the current frame as the latent action of a world model: a mind model encodes the EEG, and a world model uses it to predict the representation of a future frame, yielding a movement-grounded pretraining objective. We further introduce the Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT), which uses frame averaging to separate shared bilateral from side-specific lateral features, encoding hemispheric correspondence to reduce the burden of learning left-right relationships from data. MWM pretraining produces two models: a mind model for downstream motor decoding and a world model that can be adapted to prediction conditioned on real actions, opening a scalable and flexible path to collect egocentric data for embodied AI. Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, the mind model improves task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% relative to the strongest baseline in each task family. Compared with an inverse-dynamics latent-action baseline, the world model achieves lower prediction error and benefits 3.3 times more from matched real actions within recordings and 4.7 times more on held-out subjects.
authors: Weikang Qiu, Zheng Huang, Tinglin Huang, Yujun Yan, Rex Ying
bullets: Addresses the limited transferability of EEG motor representations learned from cue-based trials, coarse labels, or movement-agnostic objectives.
Learns from naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations by treating current EEG as a latent action that predicts future visual representations.
Introduces a Lateralization-Aware Transformer to model shared bilateral and side-specific hemispheric features.
Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, improves task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% over task-family baselines.
The world model has lower prediction error than an inverse-dynamics latent-action baseline and benefits more from matched real actions, including on held-out subjects.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Existing approaches (top) versus MWM (bottom) on the three challenges of motor EEG representation learning. (1) Cue-based trials are costly to scale, and categorical labels give one class to movements that unfold differently (Tangermann et al., 2012; Schirrmeister et al., 2017; Lawhern et al., 2018). (2) General-purpose EEG foundation models (FMs) pretrain with EEG-only objectives (Kostas et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a). MWM answers both with one mechanism: it treats the EEG recorded up to the current frame as the latent action of a world model that predicts the next visual state. It therefore learns from naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations, and its target is the visual consequence of behavior rather than the EEG itself. (3) Existing methods do not explicitly separate bilateral from lateral activity (Schirrmeister et al., 2017; Lawhern et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025a); MWM does, and pairs each horizontal video mirror with an exchange of only the lateral component Hlat.

Figure 2: The Mind World Model. (a) A frozen encoder g maps the current frame to patch features that a residual predictor advances; the same frozen g builds the target from the next frame. (b) The mind model encodes the EEG window, which ends on the current frame; its LAT encoder is detailed in Figure 3. The EEG reaches the predictor only as AdaLN modulation, never as an input token: it occupies the slot a recorded action would.

Figure 3: The Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT) for EEG encoding. (a) Patch embedding, applied within each channel, (b) the learned gate G ∈ [0, 1]C×N×De and the electrode permutation Π ∈ {0, 1}C×C , which act on the embedded tokens before any Transformer block; the mirror acts on the decomposed pair and is an involution, (c) a criss-cross block, (d) a shared Transformer with invariant and equivariant readout heads; under the mirror, Hbi is unchanged and Hlat flips sign after aligning homologous channels, and (e) the paired EEG–video mirror. Only the learned lateral component is exchanged across hemispheres; the raw signal is never permuted.

Figure 4: Lateralization analysis. (a,b) Hand-motion correlations with 95% confidence intervals estimated by bootstrap resampling, using participants as the resampling unit. (c–e) Participantaveraged motor-imagery feature-energy contrasts, normalized by channel-wise mean energy; left– right contrasts share a color scale. Control features h(1) and h(2) are equal-sized halves of h.

Table 3: Ablations of frame averaging (FA), prediction, and alignment. Balanced accuracy for classification and Pearson correlation for regression; mean ± sample s.d. over three seeds. The last row averages per-task relative changes with respect to MWM over the listed tasks.

Table 4: Evaluation of real-action conditioning in held-out next-step prediction, with IMU measurements as the action proxy. All pretrained models use the same predictor and action interface. Copy frame outputs the current frame; the action-free predictor is pretrained with the identical recipe but without EEG. Values are mean ± standard deviation from a subject-level bootstrap; 95% intervals are given in Appendix C.
Table 1: Pearson correlation on regression tasks. Mean ± sample s.d. over three seeds.
Table 2: Balanced accuracy on classification tasks. Mean ± sample s.d. over three seeds.
Table 5: Real-action conditioning with IMU windows up to the target frame only. Values are mean ± standard deviation from a subject-level bootstrap, as in Table 4.

papers.selection_reason: Treats EEG as latent action of a world model predicting future frame representations, with egocentric video learning for embodied AI.
papers.title: Mind World Models: Joint Learning of Motor EEG Representations and Action-Conditioned World Dynamics
papers.tldr: Mind World Models pretrains EEG motor representations by predicting future egocentric-video dynamics, improving motor decoding and enabling action-conditioned world-model adaptation.

papers.abstract: World models based on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn from pixels to predict the outcome of actions in a latent space. To reach a goal, a planner samples many candidate action sequences, uses the model to predict where each one leads, and executes the best one. However, standard planners draw their candidates from a Gaussian, while the model has only seen the structured, state-dependent actions of its training data. Its predictions for such candidates are unreliable, and planning fails more often as goals move farther away. We propose Skill-JEPA, which learns an action space aligned with the planner. A variational autoencoder conditioned on the current state encodes short action sequences into latent skills with a standard Gaussian prior, and decodes them back into actions. The world model predicts the effect of skills rather than raw actions, and the planner searches over skills starting from that same Gaussian, so its candidates resemble the model's training data. Skill-JEPA adds a single module, trained end-to-end with the world model, and leaves the planner untouched, with no subgoals, hierarchy, or hand-designed skills. Across three JEPA world models and four benchmarks, average success on goals 80 steps away rises from 42% with raw actions to 62%; the gains grow with goal distance and hold across four planners. On AntMaze, a quadruped locomotion task, success on goals two maze cells away rises from 0.4% to 38%. This suggests that part of the difficulty of reaching distant goals lies in the action space, and can be removed without changing the planner.
authors: Tom\'as Couso Coddou, Christ Devia, Rex G. Liu, Rodrigo Toro Icarte
bullets: Standard Gaussian action sampling produces candidates unlike the structured actions seen during training, making distant-goal planning unreliable.
A state-conditioned VAE encodes short action sequences into latent skills with a Gaussian prior and decodes them back into actions.
The world model predicts skill effects, while the unchanged planner searches over skills sampled from the same Gaussian distribution.
Across three JEPA models and four benchmarks, average success for goals 80 steps away increased from 42% to 62%.
AntMaze success for goals two cells away rose from 0.4% to 38%, with improvements growing for more distant goals.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview. papers.abstract: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.
authors: Yuxin Jiang, Wenqiang Sun, Jiaqi Li, Yuchao Gu, Lvmin Zhang, Ivor Tsang, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Addresses the challenge of learning action representations and dynamics without action labels, often requiring dynamics to be learned from scratch.
Uses one pretrained video prior for two roles: inverse dynamics via a transition encoder with learnable action queries, and forward dynamics via a causal action-conditioned generator.
Trains both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck to discover actions transferable across visual contexts and embodiments.
Achieves state-of-the-art few-shot action probing and stronger zero-shot transfer in navigation and robotic manipulation, according to the abstract.
The framework also works with predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, suggesting applicability beyond generative video models.

papers.abstract: Data assimilation (DA) in partially observed nonlinear systems requires repeated estimation of both hidden states and their uncertainty. Conventional nonlinear filtering can be computationally expensive and often relies on an explicit dynamical model. In this paper, we develop the Neural Conditional Gaussian Model (Neural CGM), a data-driven dynamical model that maps unobserved physical states into a learned latent space, where the dynamics of the latent states follow a conditional Gaussian structure. This structure allows closed-form DA updates in the latent space, while nonlinear encoder-decoder mappings retain the flexibility needed to represent complex dynamics in physical space. A key feature of Neural CGM is its treatment of uncertainty in DA. The latent posterior mean and covariance are mapped to the physical variables through a Gaussian decoder that combines local moment propagation with learned nonlinear corrections. The resulting physical-space posterior statistics depend on the sequentially updated latent distribution rather than on a separate post-processing estimate. The same statistics enter a Gaussian negative log-likelihood during training, so both the posterior mean and uncertainty affect the learned model. Because Neural CGM learns the dynamical model itself, it can also be used for state forecasting and simulation without explicit knowledge of the governing equations. Numerical experiments on benchmark nonlinear dynamical systems show accurate state estimation and forecasting while substantially reducing online assimilation cost relative to conventional nonlinear DA methods. Neural CGM is therefore suited to repeated state estimation, uncertainty quantification, and prediction from partial observations.
bullets: Addresses costly state and uncertainty estimation in partially observed nonlinear systems without requiring explicit governing equations.
Maps physical states to a latent space with conditional Gaussian dynamics, enabling closed-form sequential DA updates.
Uses a Gaussian decoder with local moment propagation and learned nonlinear corrections to produce physical-space posterior means and covariances.
Trains with a Gaussian negative log-likelihood so both state estimates and uncertainty shape the learned model.
Experiments on benchmark nonlinear systems show accurate estimation and forecasting with substantially lower online assimilation cost than conventional nonlinear DA methods.

papers.abstract: Immersive 3D content allows text and graphical elements, such as subtitles, annotations, and icons, to be placed inside a scene rather than displayed as flat overlays. Placed this way, they respect occlusion and perspective and take on user-assigned materials and lighting while preserving their original shapes. In Gaussian scenes, however, each new glyph or icon requires its own iterative optimization, which limits scalable content creation. We present FFGaussType, which converts extruded glyph and SVG outlines into Gaussian assets in a single forward pass. A point encoder maps anchors sampled on the known surface to a single feature plane, from which a decoder shared by all assets predicts neural Gaussians carrying surface normals. This separates geometric conversion from material and lighting choices, and the feature plane supports image and video coding for compact delivery. We construct a paired dataset of 27,221 glyph and SVG icon assets with anchors and calibrated normal and silhouette renderings, holding out font families for evaluation. Conversion from prepared anchors takes 9.1 ms per asset, at a fraction of the compute and memory of prior baselines. On unseen font families and test icons, FFGaussType achieves $1.62^\circ$ normal error and $0.985$ silhouette IoU, the best among the compared feed-forward converters, matching the fidelity that per-asset fitting needs thousands of steps to reach. The code and dataset will be released after publication.
authors: Haoan Feng, Tianfu Wang, Peimeng Guan, Dae Yeol Lee, Guan-ming Su
bullets: Addresses the scalability problem of iteratively optimizing every glyph or icon for Gaussian scenes.

Uses a paired dataset of 27,221 glyph and SVG icon assets, with font-family holdouts for evaluation.
Achieves 1.62° normal error and 0.985 silhouette IoU on unseen assets; conversion takes 9.1 ms per prepared asset.

papers.abstract: Latent world models predict the outcomes of action sequences, but comparing candidate plans through recursive rollout remains expensive at test time. We introduce Fast-JEPA, a latent world model planning framework that advances the success-latency Pareto frontier of predictive search. Fast-JEPA reorganizes predictive computation to support effective action-sequence search at low planning cost. It constructs a goal-directed plan to guide search and directly predicts the outcomes of complete candidates for efficient comparison, avoiding recursive state rollout during refinement. Across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, Fast-JEPA achieves 96.50% average success rate with 2.41x faster planning than INTACT. Search-budget sweeps show that its competitive success and low latency extend across candidate counts and refinement depths. We further introduce DynaGoal, a benchmark for evaluating world-model planning under dynamic out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines, and controlled response delays. Fast-JEPA achieves average success rates of 73.83% on DynaGoal-Shift and 87.67% on DynaGoal-Deadline, demonstrating the practical value of low-latency predictive planning under changing control conditions and execution-time constraints. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sofilyzia/Fast-JEPA.
authors: Yao Zhang, Bin Yu, Shijie Lian, Haishan Liu, Changti Wu, Yu Wu, Kai Chen
bullets: Targets the high test-time cost of comparing plans through recursive state prediction.
Builds a goal-directed plan and directly predicts complete candidate outcomes for efficient search refinement.

Maintains competitive success and low latency across different search budgets, candidate counts, and refinement depths.
Introduces DynaGoal to test planning under distribution shifts, deadlines, and response delays; Fast-JEPA reaches 73.83% on Shift and 87.67% on Deadline.

papers.abstract: Latent Action Models (LAMs) learn control representations from action-free video, but existing pipelines typically train latent policies with behavioral cloning, without an explicit policy improvement objective. Although offline RL offers a natural approach to policy improvement, standard methods do not transfer directly to learned latent action spaces. We find that the structure of learned latent actions makes naive offline RL unreliable: directly maximizing value over latent actions or fitting a unimodal policy can produce latent actions that cannot be realized by physical execution, while the latent representation can merge physical controls that receive different rewards. To understand when latent-space optimization remains valid, we derive conditions under which policy improvement transfers to decoded execution and under which latent and physical optima align. Building on these insights, we propose LAPIS for goal-conditioned latent policy improvement, grounding value-based policy improvement in observed state-latent transitions and using a conditional flow policy to capture their multimodal structure. LAPIS outperforms baselines on most tasks, with the clearest gains in visual manipulation, and remains effective even with only 1% action labels, where competing methods largely collapse.
authors: Donghyeon Ki, Xiaoyu Chen, Jun Ho Seo, Hayeong Lee, Kyungyoon Kim, Byung-Jun Lee, Li Zhao
bullets: Latent Action Models usually use behavioral cloning, lacking an explicit policy-improvement objective.
Naive offline RL can propose unrealizable latent actions or merge physical controls with different rewards.
The paper derives conditions for policy improvement and optimality to transfer from latent actions to physical execution.
LAPIS uses observed state–latent transitions, value-based improvement, and a conditional flow policy for multimodal latent actions.
It outperforms baselines on most tasks, especially visual manipulation, and remains effective with only 1% action labels.
